title: Brad and Noah discuss the reindustrialization of America
gist: Podcast notes (Hexapodia ep. 65) in which Noah Smith and Brad DeLong argue US reindustrialization should be justified by geopolitics and security, not by a return of mass blue-collar factory jobs, and that America mainly lacks two things: land use/permitting reform and bank finance. Smith floats selective Dodd-Frank exemptions so the megabanks can fund manufacturing.

insights.claim: Noah Smith and Brad DeLong list three rationales for boosting US manufacturing: geopolitical/military supply-chain independence from China, growth via agglomeration and clustering effects, and economic equality through blue-collar jobs.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Policy support for manufacturing will increasingly be framed and funded as national security, favoring defense and dual-use supply chains.
insights.locator: Basically, there are three main reasons

insights.claim: A US defense and dual-use manufacturing supply chain not dominated by China is needed both to be able to fight a war with China and to avoid being bullied by Chinese export controls.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Supports sustained policy tailwinds for domestic defense/dual-use suppliers and non-China supply chains.
insights.quote: China has shown themselves perfectly willing to use export controls to bully other countries (including ours)

insights.claim: Smith and DeLong judge that reindustrializing to create mass semi-skilled factory employment is a dead end because AI and AI-driven robotics will mostly automate manufacturing.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: New US factories will be capex- and automation-heavy rather than labor-heavy; robotics and automation vendors benefit more than labor.
insights.quote: the era of mass semi-skilled blue-collar factory employment is simply over and done

insights.claim: Automated factories can still create jobs indirectly through a local multiplier effect on local service employment, but only if the people running the factories live nearby and spend locally.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Regional economic impact of reshoring depends on where managers/engineers live, not factory headcount.

insights.claim: Ukraine is cited as the one known example of a country that successfully reindustrialized, by building a strong drone and robotics industry out of wartime necessity against Russia.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Suggests drones/robotics are the most plausible reindustrialization vector, driven by military demand.

themes.theme: Binding constraints: land use and bank loans

insights.claim: Smith and DeLong tentatively conclude America lacks only two important things to reindustrialize: land use (permitting) and bank loans.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Watch permitting legislation and bank-regulation changes as the key catalysts for US manufacturing buildout.
insights.quote: America really lacks only two important things — land use, and bank loans

insights.claim: Bank finance is important for manufacturing and is an area where America struggles compared with other countries.

insights.claim: Noah Smith proposes using America's 'moribund' megabanks as pools of capital for reindustrialization by granting them selective exemptions from post-2008 Dodd-Frank restrictions.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: A policy idea that, if adopted, would expand large-bank lending capacity and could be a positive for big US bank stocks.
